p: The oldest manuscripts say "loved" by God the Father. Later ones, and the KJV, say "sanctified."

readings.w: Papyrus 72 (about AD 300), Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and Alexandrinus (300s–400s); NA28, SBLGNT
Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "sanctified by God the Father")

why: "Loved" has much the older and wider support. "Loved in God" is an unusual phrase, and a copyist could easily change it to the more familiar "sanctified in God" (compare 1 Corinthians 1:2). The reverse change is hard to explain.
b: The two Greek words look alike (ēgapēmenois, hēgiasmenois). Jude's letter is full of love language: "beloved" (1:3, 17, 20), "love feasts" (1:12), "the love of God" (1:21), so "loved" fits his style.

a: our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ
p: Later manuscripts add "God," so the KJV reads "the only Lord God, and our Lord Jesus Christ."

readings.w: Papyrus 72, Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Alexandrinus and Ephraemi; NA28, SBLGNT
readings.orig: τὸν μόνον δεσπότην καὶ κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν
readings.en: our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ
readings.plain: our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ

readings.w: Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: τὸν μόνον δεσπότην θεὸν καὶ κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν
readings.en: the only Master, God, and our Lord Jesus Christ
readings.plain: the only Master, God, and our Lord Jesus Christ

why: The oldest manuscripts lack "God." It was probably added because "only Master" (despotēs) was normally a title for God, and copyists wanted to make that explicit.
b: Without "God," both titles, Master and Lord, clearly belong to Jesus, because one Greek article governs both. With "God," the KJV can read two persons: God the Master, and our Lord Jesus Christ. Some defenders of the KJV argue the reverse, that "God" was removed, but there is no early evidence for it. Either way Jesus is called Lord.

p: The hardest variant in Jude. The oldest manuscripts say Jesus saved the people out of Egypt.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus and Vaticanus (300s–400s), minuscules 33, 81, 1739, the Latin Vulgate, Coptic versions; NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT. English: ESV, CSB, NLT, NET, NRSVue, BSB
Codex Sinaiticus (300s), Codex Ephraemi (400s), Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus; NA27, Westcott and Hort. English: KJV, NKJV, NIV, NASB, NABRE
A few later manuscripts
Papyrus 72 (about AD 300)

why: "Jesus" is the reading of some of the oldest and best manuscripts and of early translations, and it is the harder reading: a copyist who found "Jesus" in an Exodus story would be tempted to change it to "the Lord," while it is hard to see why anyone would change "the Lord" to "Jesus." Papyrus 72's "God Christ" also points to a reading that named Christ.
b: Ancient copies abbreviated sacred names, and ΙΣ (Jesus) and ΚΣ (Lord) differ by one letter, so an accidental change is possible in either direction. In the 1970s, the committee of the UBS Greek New Testament chose "the Lord" by a majority. Bruce Metzger and Allen Wikgren dissented: they judged "Jesus" the best-attested reading, difficult as it is. In 2012–2013 the editors of NA28 and of the Editio Critica Maior, the large new critical edition, changed the text to "Jesus." Recent English revisions have been moving toward "Jesus": the NRSV (1989) read "the Lord," and its 2021 update (NRSVue) reads "Jesus." See also the next manuscript note, on where "once" goes.

a: all this once and for all
p: Copies put "once" with "you know" or with "Jesus saved." The Byzantine text reads "this" for "all this."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus and others; SBLGNT, NA27, Westcott and Hort
readings.en: knowing all things once for all
readings.plain: all this once and for all

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus, Vaticanus and others; NA28, Editio Critica Maior
readings.orig: εἰδότας ὑμᾶς πάντα ὅτι Ἰησοῦς ἅπαξ
readings.en: knowing all things, that Jesus once (saved)

readings.w: Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "though ye once knew this")

why: The Plain English Translation follows its base text, the SBLGNT. The NA28 order is a strong rival: there "once" goes with "saved" ("Jesus once saved a people... and the second time destroyed"), a neat contrast with "the second time" (to deuteron). If you switch to the NA28 reading, read the rest of the verse as "Jesus once saved a people... and later destroyed."
b: The meaning hardly changes: Jude is reminding, not teaching anything new.

t: All the ungodly, or every person?
p: Some old manuscripts say Enoch's Lord will convict "every soul," like 1 Enoch's "all flesh."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, Alexandrinus and most manuscripts; SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott and Hort, Byzantine majority (adding "among them"), Textus Receptus (KJV)
Papyrus 72, Codex Sinaiticus; NA27, NA28

why: This follows the SBLGNT, the base text for the Plain English Translation. The editions disagree. NA28 prefers "every soul," which agrees with 1 Enoch's own wording ("all flesh") and is the less repetitive reading; the SBLGNT prefers the reading of most manuscripts, which keeps Jude's four-fold "ungodly."
b: The difference is small in meaning: either the Lord convicts everyone, or he convicts all the ungodly. It is a good example of how carefully editors weigh a few very old manuscripts against many slightly younger ones.

a: Have mercy on some, those who waver.
p: Goes with the next manuscript note on verse 23. Manuscripts give two groups, three, or different verbs.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus and others; NA28, SBLGNT (three groups)
readings.en: and have mercy on some who waver
readings.plain: Have mercy on some, those who waver.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus and others; Tyndale House GNT, Tregelles (three groups)
Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "of some have compassion, making a difference")
readings.en: and have mercy on some, making a distinction
readings.plain: Have mercy on some, making a distinction.

readings.w: Papyrus 72 (about AD 300), short form (two groups)
readings.plain: Grab some out of the fire.

why: The three-part text has strong, early support, and it fits Jude's love of threes (three warnings in 1:5–7, three sinners in 1:11). Repeating "have mercy" twice is awkward, which may be why copyists shortened or changed it. The Plain English Translation follows the SBLGNT and NA28. Switch verse 23 to the matching reading as well.
b: Codex Vaticanus has yet another two-part form, and Douglas Moo counts at least six forms in all. Richard Bauckham argues for a two-clause text like Papyrus 72's, which he translates "Snatch some from the fire; but on those who dispute have mercy with fear." Alexandrinus's "correct" (elenchete) avoids the double "have mercy" and echoes Enoch's "convict" (the same verb, Jude 15).

a: Rescue others: grab them out of the fire. On still others have mercy, but with fear,
p: Goes with the manuscript note on verse 22: is "with fear" about rescuing, or about mercy for a third group?

p: The KJV's "only wise God" adds "wise," probably from Romans 16:27.

readings.w: Papyrus 72, Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Alexandrinus; NA28, SBLGNT
Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV)

why: The oldest manuscripts lack "wise." Copyists likely added it from the similar doxology in Romans 16:27, "to the only wise God," which they knew well.

p: The oldest manuscripts give glory to God "through Jesus Christ." The Byzantine text and KJV lack it.

readings.w: Papyrus 72, Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Alexandrinus; NA28, SBLGNT
readings.orig: διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν

readings.w: Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV)

why: The phrase has the oldest support. Some suggest later copyists dropped it because giving glory "through" Jesus seemed to make him less than God, an issue in the debates of the 300s.

p: The oldest manuscripts praise God's glory "before every age" too. The KJV has only "now and ever."

readings.w: Papyrus 72, Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Alexandrinus; NA28, SBLGNT
Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV)

why: The phrase has the oldest support, and it is unusual: doxologies normally look only forward ("now and forever"), so copyists would be more likely to drop it than to add it.
